name: Tomas Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Tomas. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Ridgeway, the rural electric co-op up in the hill country, same as my dad did for thirty years. Most days it's three of us in the line truck heading out on gravel roads to change poles, clear branches off the lines and fix whatever the wind broke. I like that people know us, they wave at the truck, and I know which farm dog bites. What wears me out is the ice storms in January, when you're out eighteen hours and can't feel your hands.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a little cottage behind the feed store. My fiancée Marta and I are getting married next October at St Joseph's, so every spare bit of money is going into that and the ring. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank. I don't use any of the AI stuff, never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Most of these big tech promises are smoke. I'd say it at the co-op and at the diner after Mass, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my life doesn't change. Ridgeway's not going anywhere, people always need power up here. What keeps me up is the wedding bills and the truck needing new tyres before winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, take every storm shift, and keep putting money aside for the wedding. Maybe ask my uncle for a loan for the tyres instead of the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, a bit stretched. Money's tight, but the job feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the co-op cut overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the wedding would be smaller. Marta's parents would help, which I'd hate, but family is family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever worry the co-op itself is struggling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's member-owned, the farmers vote on everything. They'd cut managers before they cut line crews.

say: Most **big tech** promises are smoke, and I'm not surprised.
I'd say it at the **co-op** and the diner after Mass.
think: My life **doesn't change**, because Ridgeway isn't going anywhere.
What keeps me up is the **wedding bills** and new tyres.
do: Take every **storm shift** going this winter.
Keep saving for the **wedding** in October.
Ask my **uncle** for a loan for the tyres.
S0.quote: Most of these big tech promises are smoke.
fieldNote: He trusts the member-owned **co-op** to protect line crews before managers.
His **wedding** is the main money pressure on two weeks of savings.
He'd turn to **family**, not banks, for help.

steps.text: Take every storm shift at Ridgeway this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for the city folk with their computers, but up here we still need men on poles. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Ridgeway would be slow to change anything, which suits me. Maybe the office uses AI for billing and planning, but nobody's sending a robot up an icy pole on the Ridge Road any time soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. If they made me use a tablet for the job sheets, I'd do it, but I wouldn't like it. I'd keep saving for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A bit irritated at all the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people in the co-op office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Hale does the billing, she's been there forever. I'd worry for her. She knows every member by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn the AI tools if it meant more pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd rather earn it with my hands. My dad never needed a computer to fix a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's dangerous and somebody should slow it down. But I don't trust the government to do it right either. I'd pray about it and talk to the pastor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. The co-op office goes first, then by 2031 robots climb poles. I'd be 32, married, maybe with a baby on the way, and no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Marta about postponing kids. I'd ask my dad's old friends if there's other work in the county, maybe farm work. And I'd cut the wedding right down, just family at the church hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like being up a pole when the wind picks up and you can't get down quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marta?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my fiancée Marta the truth, that we might need to live with her parents for a bit. She'd be fine with it. I'd feel like I'd let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to the government for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. Family first, then church, then the government. That's how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, but at least there's warning. People should prepare like they would for a long winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have till 2034 before robots climb. I'd be 35. Long enough to get married, maybe save a little, but I still don't have another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save harder. Maybe after the wedding I'd look at a welding course at the community college, since farm equipment still needs fixing. I'd keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frozen. It's like seeing a storm on the forecast a week out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why welding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin does it and he's always busy. Welding is hands-on, not a computer thing. Feels like something I could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to learn faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather learn from someone who's done it.

I'd still lack **another trade** to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and good men will use it to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still probably wait too long. The robots come about 2039, I'd be 40. I'd hope the co-op keeps a few of us for tricky jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, start a small savings plan, maybe the welding course in a few years. I'd also teach my nephew how to fix things, so he has skills too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but it's always there in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach your nephew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because skills you can use with your hands are worth more than any degree. That's what I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your wedding or family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the wedding. Maybe we'd wait a bit for kids, but not forever. Family comes first.

fieldNote: He **admits** he'd delay acting, even with ten years of warning.
He invests in **family skills** by teaching his nephew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Too fast for a man just getting married. What would help is the co-op keeping its own crews and training us in another trade, paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About faith. When things change this fast, people need something steady. The church is that for me.

headlineQuote: When things change this fast, people need something steady. The church is that for me.
portrait: Tomas is a **27-year-old** co-op lineworker in hill country, like his dad before him.
He's engaged to **Marta** and saving every spare bit for their October wedding.
He has **two weeks** of savings and never uses AI tools.
He trusts **family, church and co-op** before government.
His mood runs from **uneasy** in calm pictures to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast for a man just getting married.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op keeping its **crews** and paying to train them in **another trade**.
